transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's just... I'm here because my sleep has been completely broken for a really long time now. I mean, it feels like it's been ages since I actually got a good night's rest. I work as a home health aide, so my days are physically and emotionally draining, and by the time I get home, I am just utterly exhausted. I literally fall into bed, thinking I'll just pass out, but then it's like my brain just won't turn off, or maybe my body is just too wired. I end up waking up to every single little sound in the house—the floorboards creaking, the wind outside, even just the hum of the refrigerator. It's like I'm on high alert all night long. And then, to make matters worse, I always end up waking up way before my alarm even goes off. I'll just lie there in the dark, watching the clock, feeling just as tired as when I went to sleep. It's like I never really rested at all, and then I have to get up and do the whole exhausting day all over again. It's just wearing me down to the bone.
Have you experienced any particularly stressful or traumatic events recently?

Well, no, not really. I mean, people always ask that, like there must be some big, terrible thing that just happened, you know? Like a car accident or someone passing away suddenly, or a divorce, but honestly... there's really nothing like that. My life is pretty much just exactly the same as it always is. 

I get up, I go to my clients—and, I mean, don't get me wrong, being a home health aide has its moments where it's tough. You're lifting people, you're helping them bathe, and you're dealing with their families. And sometimes those families can be very demanding, always asking why this wasn't done or why that wasn't done perfectly. But I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, so it's not like it's a *new* stress, if that makes sense? It's just my normal, everyday routine. 

I haven't lost anyone recently, I haven't moved, there are no big financial disasters... well, other than just the usual bills we all have to pay, but nothing out of the ordinary. So, no, I really can't point to one specific thing that just happened to set all this off. I was actually thinking about that the other day when I was lying awake at 3 AM, just staring at the ceiling and wondering, "Why is my brain doing this?" I went through everything in my head, trying to find a reason, but there really isn't anything new or traumatic. It's just the same old daily grind, which is why it's so frustrating that I suddenly can't seem to sleep through it anymore.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge during the day, not just when you're trying to sleep?

No, not really... I mean, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or on edge during the day. It's funny you ask that, because my sister, she's a very anxious person, you know? She's always worrying about everything—what she said to the cashier at the grocery store, if she left the stove on, all that kind of stuff. And I see how she gets, how wound up she is all day long, and I'm just not like that. 

During the day, I'm mostly just... well, tired. Like I said, I'm dragging myself from one client's house to the next. I'm focusing on getting them out of bed, making sure they take their pills, making sure they eat something, and just trying to keep my eyes open while I'm doing it. I don't really have the energy to feel anxious, if that makes sense. I'm just kind of going through the motions, feeling heavy and worn out. 

It's really just when I finally lay down in bed that the trouble starts. That's when I get that wired feeling, where every little noise makes me jump. But during the day? No, I'm not on edge. I'm just exhausted and, honestly, just feeling kind of down and flat because I have no energy to do anything else. I just want to get through my shift so I can go home and try to rest, even though I know the resting part probably isn't going to happen. So, yeah, no daytime anxiety, just the exhaustion and that heavy, dragging feeling all day long.
Do you often feel sad or hopeless during the day?

Well... yeah, I guess I do. It's not like a sudden, sharp sadness, you know? It's more like... like everything is just kind of muted. I was actually trying to explain this to my daughter the other day. I told her it's like the color has just completely drained out of everything. 

Even when I'm doing things that I know I should be enjoying, or that I *used* to enjoy. Like, we always have this big Sunday dinner with the whole family—my kids, my grandkids, my sister. Usually, it's this loud, happy thing, and I used to love cooking for it and setting everything up. But lately, I'm just sitting there at the head of the table, looking at everyone laughing and passing the potatoes, and I just feel... nothing. Or just this heavy, dull feeling. And it's the same with other things, too. I used to really love looking at art, you know? I took a few art history classes back when I was in college—just some community college classes, but I really loved them. I have these beautiful prints hanging in my hallway, and I used to stop and just admire the brushstrokes and the colors. Now, I walk right past them and they just look like flat pieces of paper on the wall. 

And the strangest part is, while I'm feeling so numb to all the good stuff, I also find myself having to fight back tears for absolutely no reason at all. I'll just be driving to a client's house, or folding laundry, or standing in the grocery store aisle looking at the canned beans, and suddenly my throat gets all tight and my eyes well up. And I have to take these deep breaths and blink really hard and tell myself, "Stop it, there's nothing to cry about, pull yourself together." It takes so much effort just to keep from crying right there in the middle of Aisle 4. So, yes, I suppose I do feel sad, but it's just this constant, heavy, gray kind of sad that never really lifts. It's just always there, dragging right alongside me all day long.
Do you find yourself no longer enjoying activities that you once found pleasurable?

Well, I... I think I kind of just mentioned that, actually. About the Sunday dinners and the art prints in my hallway? I mean, I really don't want to repeat myself too much, but yes, that's exactly what's happening. The things I used to love just don't do anything for me anymore. 

Like I was saying about the Sunday dinners... I used to spend the whole weekend planning the menu, going to three different grocery stores just to get the right kind of roast or the freshest vegetables. I loved the whole process of it, the chopping, the simmering, the smells filling up the house. And then having everyone sit down together, the kids running around, my sister talking my ear off about whatever was going on at her job... it used to fill me up, you know? It made all the hard work during the week feel worth it. But now... now it just feels like another chore. Another thing on my endless list of things to do. I still cook, because, well, they expect it and I don't want to let them down, but I don't get any joy out of it. I just go through the motions, chopping the carrots, roasting the meat, setting the table, and I'm just exhausted and empty the whole time. 

And it's not just the big things, either. It's the little things, too. Like, I used to love having a cup of tea in the morning before work. Just sitting by the window, watching the neighborhood wake up, feeling the warmth of the mug in my hands. It was my quiet time, my little moment of peace before the chaos of the day started. Now, I just gulp it down while I'm rushing to get my uniform on, not even tasting it, just needing the caffeine to keep my eyes open. Or reading... I used to read a lot, mostly mystery novels, you know, the kind you get at the grocery store checkout. I could get lost in them for hours. But lately, I can't even focus on a single page. I read the same paragraph over and over, and nothing sticks. It's just words on a page. So, yeah, I guess I'd say I'm definitely not enjoying the things I used to. It's like someone just turned down the volume on my whole life, and everything is just... flat.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because I don't actually own a scale. I threw mine out years ago, back when my kids were still in high school, because I just didn't want to obsess over numbers, you know? But... yes, I think I have lost some weight. I haven't been trying to, not at all, but my clothes are definitely fitting a lot differently lately. 

Like, my work scrubs? The pants have this drawstring, and I'm having to pull it so much tighter now just to keep them up while I'm bending over to help my clients out of bed or into the shower. And my regular clothes, too, they're just... they're just hanging looser on me. I think it's mostly because my appetite is pretty much completely gone. 

Like I was saying about those Sunday dinners—I'll make this huge spread, a big roast, mashed potatoes, the green beans, the whole nine yards. And everyone else is eating and laughing and going back for seconds, and I'll just put a little bit on my plate and sort of... push it around. I just pick at whatever I make for everyone else. Nothing really sounds good or tastes good anymore. And then during the week, by the time I finish my shift and finally drag myself home, the thought of actually making a real meal for myself is just too much. I can't even fathom standing at the stove. So I usually just pop a piece of bread in the toaster. I'll just eat a piece of toast, maybe put a little butter on it if I have the energy, and that's it for the night. So, yeah, between having no appetite and just eating toast or picking at leftovers, the weight is definitely coming off, even though I'm really not trying to lose it.
Do you often feel guilty about things?

Guilty? No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I know some people get really down on themselves and feel like everything is their fault, but that's not really what's happening with me. I don't sit around feeling bad about things I've done in the past, or like I'm a terrible person or anything like that. 

I mean, sure, I feel bad that I'm not as fun to be around anymore, like with my grandkids. I used to be the one getting down on the floor and playing board games with them, or taking them out to the park. Now I just sort of sit in the armchair and watch them. And I guess I feel a little guilty that I'm not the grandma I used to be, but it's not this overwhelming, crushing guilt that keeps me up at night. It's more just... a sad realization that I don't have the energy for it. 

And with work, too. I try my best with my clients, I really do. I make sure they're clean and fed and safe, but I know I'm not as chatty or as cheerful as I used to be. Mrs. Higgins, one of my regulars, she used to love it when I'd come over because we'd gossip about the neighborhood and watch her daytime stories together. Now, I just do what I need to do and sit quietly while the TV is on. I feel bad that I can't be that bright spot in her day anymore, but again, it's not really guilt. I haven't done anything wrong, you know? I haven't hurt anyone or made any terrible mistakes that I'm obsessing over. It's just that I'm so tired and empty, and I feel bad that other people have to deal with this version of me. But actual guilt? No, I don't think I have that. I'm just trying to get through the day, honestly.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it's... it's been a really long time. Honestly, it feels like it's just become my normal now, which is a scary thought, but... yeah. If I really think back on when the shift happened, when things started getting so heavy and flat, it was right around the time my mother-in-law moved in with us. That was a little over two years ago now. 

My husband and I, we'd had the house to ourselves for a bit after the kids finally got settled on their own, and we were just getting used to that quiet, you know? And then she had her fall, and she couldn't stay in her apartment anymore, and of course, since I'm a home health aide, everyone just sort of looked at me like, "Well, you're the professional, you know how to handle this." And I do, I really do know how to care for people, but doing it all day at work and then coming home and doing it all night... it just changed everything in the house. 

The dynamic shifted. Suddenly, our living room was full of medical equipment, and the TV was always blaring because she's hard of hearing, and I was constantly on edge, listening for her to call out. I think that's when this whole cloud just sort of settled over me. At first, I thought I was just adjusting to the new routine, you know, just tired from the extra work. But then the months went by, and she got more settled, and we got a routine down, but I never bounced back. The tiredness just stayed, and then the joy started seeping out of things, like I told you about the dinners and my morning tea. So, yeah, it's been a solid two years, maybe a little more, of just feeling like I'm wading through mud every single day. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, like the woman who used to love planning those big Sunday meals, but... it's been over two years now, and she just hasn't come back.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you used to enjoy?

Lost interest? Hmm. No, I don't really think so. I mean, I still really care about the things I've always liked doing. 

Like, for example, I've been a big scrapbooker for... oh, gosh, it has to be going on fifteen years now. I started right around the time my oldest son graduated high school because I wanted to make him this huge memory book for his graduation party, with all his sports photos and his report cards and everything. And I still love it. I really do. I still get the craft catalogs in the mail, and I'll sit there at the kitchen table and circle all the new patterned papers and the little die-cut stickers I want to get. 

Just the other day, actually, I was at the craft store—I had to run out to get some more of those little double-sided adhesive squares because I was running low on my favorite brand—and I ended up spending probably forty-five minutes just looking at all the new seasonal stamps. They had these beautiful autumn ones with the little acorns and the metallic foil leaves, and I was just so engaged looking at them, thinking about how I could use them for the photos from last Thanksgiving. I even bought a few new ink pads. 

So the interest is definitely still there. I still want to do it, and I still love looking at other people's layouts online. I'm in this Facebook group for scrapbookers, and I check it every single morning while I'm waiting for my toast to pop up. I love seeing what everyone is working on, and I still leave comments and save ideas to my own folders. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest at all. The desire to do it and the love for the hobby is still exactly the same as it's always been. I still have my whole craft rolling cart set up right in the corner of the living room, right where I can see it, with all my special scissors and markers color-coded. So, yeah, no, the interest hasn't gone anywhere at all.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past few months?

Weight? Well, yes, actually. I have lost some weight, but it's not like I've been on a diet or trying to do it on purpose. I actually first noticed it a few weeks ago with my work clothes. I wear these navy blue scrubs for my home health visits, and usually, they fit pretty snug around the waist, especially since I'm sitting in the car driving from client to client. But over the last couple of months, I've had to pull the drawstrings tighter and tighter, and they're just hanging loose off me now. Even my regular weekend jeans, the ones I wear when I'm just running to the grocery store or the pharmacy for my mother-in-law, they're so baggy I had to dig out an old belt from the back of the closet just to keep them up. 

And it's really just because I don't have much of an appetite anymore. Nothing sounds good. I still cook, of course, because I have to make dinner for my husband and my mother-in-law. I'll stand there and make a whole meal—like the other night, I made this big baked ziti with the Italian sausage, which used to be my absolute favorite—but when we actually sit down at the table, I just end up picking at it. I'll push the pasta around my plate and maybe take a bite or two just so my husband doesn't fuss at me, but I just don't have the stomach for a full meal. It all just seems so heavy. 

And then during the day, after my shift, when I come home from taking care of my clients, I used to sit down and have a proper lunch, maybe a sandwich or some leftover soup. Now? I just can't be bothered to put anything together or even chew a real meal. I'll usually just grab a piece of toast. Just pop a slice of plain wheat bread in the toaster, maybe put a little scrape of butter on it if I'm feeling up to it, and eat it standing over the sink. It's just easy, you know? So I guess between just living on a piece of toast here and there and picking at whatever I make for everyone else, the weight has just been falling off without me even trying. Some women my age would probably be thrilled to drop a few sizes without going to the gym, but for me, it just feels strange, like my clothes don't even belong to me anymore.
Do you feel pleasure when engaging in activities that you normally enjoy?

Pleasure? Hmm. That’s… well, that’s a different question, isn't it? I was just telling you how I still have all the interest in the world, how I still buy the supplies and set everything up. But actual pleasure... no, I really don't think I feel that anymore. Not like I used to. 

Like, if I go back to the scrapbooking… I’ll get everything out on a Sunday afternoon, right? I’ll clear off the kitchen table, push my mother-in-law’s pill organizers to the side, wipe down the placemats, and I’ll pull my rolling cart over. I’ll have all my new autumn stamps and the metallic foil leaves I just bought, and I’ll sit there with the photos from last Thanksgiving. I want to do it, I really do. But when I actually start stamping the paper and using my double-sided tape to stick the photos down… it’s just flat. I don't feel anything. 

I used to get this little… I don't know, this little thrill or spark in my chest when a layout came together perfectly. I’d hold the page up to the light and just feel so proud and happy about how the colors matched and how I'd preserved that memory for my kids. Now, I’ll finish a whole two-page spread, and I just look at it and think, "Okay, well, that’s done." There’s no warmth to it at all. No satisfaction. 

And it’s the exact same thing with the cooking I mentioned earlier. I told you about the baked ziti. I used to genuinely love the process of making it. The smell of the garlic and the onions sautéing in the olive oil used to make me so happy, it would just instantly relax me after a long day of driving from client to client. But now, I stand there stirring the pot, smelling the garlic, and it’s just… a smell. It doesn't bring me any joy. It just feels like I'm going through the motions of being me. I keep doing these things because they're my hobbies, they're what I'm supposed to enjoy, but that actual feeling of pleasure? No, I haven't noticed that in a very, very long time. I just sit there with my scissors and my paper, or my wooden spoon at the stove, waiting to feel happy about it, and it just never happens.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from things that would normally bring you happiness?

Well, yes, exactly. I mean... I think that's really what I was just trying to get at with the scrapbooking and the cooking. I'm sorry, I don't mean to repeat myself, it's just... yes, that's exactly it. "Unable" is probably the perfect word for it. 

It's like the switch is just broken. I know I *should* feel happy about things. I have a good life, you know? My husband is a good man, he really is, even if he doesn't quite understand why I'm so quiet lately. And my oldest son, the one I mentioned with the graduation scrapbook? He just called us last weekend to tell us he got a promotion at the logistics company he works for. And normally, oh my goodness, normally I would have been over the moon. I would have been planning a celebratory dinner, maybe making a special cake, calling my sister in Ohio to brag about him... but when he told me on the phone, I just sort of... I just said, "Oh, that's nice, honey, good for you." And we hung up and I just sat there on the couch. 

I knew it was happy news, but I couldn't *feel* the happiness. It's like I'm completely unable to absorb it anymore. It's incredibly frustrating, to be honest with you. You sit there waiting for the joy to kick in, because you know this is a happy moment, or you know you're doing a happy activity, but it just stays entirely flat. It's like watching a movie of someone else's life. You see the happy things happening, you know they're supposed to bring you joy, but you're just watching it all happen through a thick pane of glass. So, yes, to answer your question, I just can't seem to feel it at all, no matter how hard I try to force it.
How long have you felt like you couldn't experience pleasure from things that normally bring you happiness?

How long? Well... let me think. It’s actually pretty easy to pinpoint the timeline, because I know exactly when things started shifting for me. It wasn't just a gradual thing where I woke up one random Tuesday and realized I felt flat. It’s been going on since my mother-in-law moved in with us, which was a little over two years ago now. 

Before that, she was living in her own little condo on the east side of town, doing just fine, really. But then she had this terrible fall. She slipped right on her kitchen linoleum and couldn't get up for hours. After she finally got out of the physical rehab center, it just wasn't safe for her to be living completely on her own anymore. And, you know, since I do home health care for a living, my husband and I just looked at each other and knew it made the most sense for her to come to us and take the spare bedroom. We had the space since the boys had moved out, so we didn't really have a good excuse not to. But I have to tell you, it completely changed the entire atmosphere of the house. 

At first, I just thought I was exhausted from the transition. I mean, I was working my regular shifts, driving all over the county taking care of my clients, and then coming home to basically do the exact same job for her—managing her pill organizers, getting her meals ready, making sure she was comfortable. It was a lot. But even after we finally got into a steady routine and the physical exhaustion sort of settled down, that joy just never came back. 

So it's been a little over two solid years of this. Two whole years of setting up my scrapbook paper or cooking a nice meal and just feeling absolutely nothing. It's like the weekend we moved her boxes into that spare room, my ability to actually enjoy my own life just got packed away too. It's been a long two years of just going through the motions like that.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or the way you move throughout the day?

Energy levels? Oh, goodness... yes. Yes, absolutely. It’s actually been a real struggle lately. I mean, my days have always been long, but it feels so different now. You know I do home health care, so I'm usually out the door by 6:30 or 7:00 in the morning, driving all over the county. And it's physical work, too—helping people out of bed, assisting with showers, transferring them from the bed to their recliners. I have one client, Mr. Abernathy, who is a fairly large man, and helping him takes a lot out of me. But I used to handle it all just fine. I used to have the stamina for it.

Now, though... by the time I finish seeing my home-health clients for the day and I pull into my own driveway, I usually just sit in the car for a few minutes. I just sit there with the engine off because I know I have to go inside and start helping out at home with my mother-in-law. And when I finally make myself get out of the car and walk through that front door, my body just feels so incredibly heavy. That's the only way I can describe it. Like my arms and legs are filled with wet sand or lead. 

It gets to the point where even the smallest, most basic tasks feel like climbing a mountain. I have to do my charting every evening, you know, writing up my notes for the agency on my tablet so they have a record of the clients' vitals and everything. I used to just sit at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and knock it out in fifteen minutes. Now, even just opening the app and charting those notes can feel like entirely too much to push through. I'll just stare at the screen, resting my head in my hand, feeling like I can't even type. 

And the laundry! Oh, the laundry. Between my husband's work clothes and my mother-in-law's things, there is always a basket waiting. I'll look at a pile of clean towels on the sofa—just simple folding, right? Nothing strenuous at all. But I just look at it and feel like I physically cannot lift my arms to fold a single washcloth. The energy just isn't there anymore. I just feel so weighed down and completely drained, like I'm dragging myself through mud just to get through the evening.
Have you noticed any changes in your symptoms over the past few months, either getting better or worse?

Well, let me think about the last few months specifically. You know, since maybe around the holidays? It's... it's hard to say, really, because all the days just seem to bleed together lately. But to answer your question, no, I wouldn't say things have gotten worse, but they certainly haven't gotten any better either. It's just this constant, flat line. Every single day feels exactly the same. I wake up, I go see my clients, I come home to my mother-in-law, I stare at the laundry... it's honestly a bit like that movie Groundhog Day, if you've ever seen it. Just waking up and doing the exact same heavy, exhausting routine without any spark of joy, day in and day out. 

I keep hoping, you know, that maybe with the seasons changing, or maybe if I just got one solid, uninterrupted night of sleep things might lift a little. My mother-in-law, she gets up a lot in the night to use the restroom, and she has one of those aluminum walkers with the tennis balls on the back legs? And our hallway is hardwood, so I can hear that *scuff, scuff, scuff* sound at 2 AM, and once I'm awake, I'm just awake, staring at the ceiling, thinking about everything I have to do the next day. But even on the rare nights where she actually sleeps straight through till dawn, I still wake up feeling just as drained and just as numb as I always do. 

So, no, I haven't noticed any real shift up or down in how I'm feeling. It's just a steady plateau of... well, of nothingness, really. Just this heavy nothingness that doesn't budge an inch. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, maybe just one day where I feel a little lighter or have a little more pep in my step, but it just hasn't happened. It's been remarkably, frustratingly consistent.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that aren't there when you're alone?

Voices? Or seeing things? Oh, no, no. Goodness, no. Nothing like that. I mean, honestly, Doctor, I’m rarely ever truly alone to even know what that would be like! Between driving to my clients' houses all day and then coming home to my husband and my mother-in-law, there is almost always someone talking to me or needing something from me. 

But no, when I am actually by myself—like in the car on the drive home, which is about the only twenty minutes of peace I get all day—it’s just quiet. Well, I say quiet, but usually I'm just sitting there listening to the hum of the engine or the radio playing softly in the background, just going over the grocery list in my head or trying to figure out when I'm going to find time to pick up my mother-in-law's blood pressure prescriptions. But as for hearing people talking who aren't there, or seeing things? No. 

I actually have a couple of clients in my home health work—older folks, mostly the ones further along with dementia—who do experience that sort of thing. I had this one sweet lady last year, Mrs. Higgins, who used to talk to her late husband in the corner of the living room the entire time I was fixing her lunch. She would point right at the armchair and ask him if he wanted a sandwich. So I've seen what that looks like firsthand, and I know exactly what you're asking about, but I've never experienced anything like that myself. My mind is just... well, it's just heavy with my own thoughts, but they're definitely just my own thoughts. Just the regular, exhausting worries of the day, nothing out of the ordinary like that.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your loved ones?

A burden? Oh, goodness... no. No, I wouldn't say I feel like a burden. Honestly, it's quite the opposite. I'm the one carrying everyone else, you know? I mean, my husband works hard, he really does, he's at the auto parts store all day, but when he gets home, he's just done. He sits in his recliner, turns on the evening news, and that's it for him. He doesn't really notice what needs doing around the house. And then there's his mother, my mother-in-law, who lives with us. I love her, I really do, but she needs so much help. She can't stand at the stove to cook anymore, she needs help getting her compression socks on in the mornings, and like I mentioned, she's up and down all night with that walker. 

So, no, I don't feel like a burden to them because I'm the one making sure they have clean clothes, hot meals, and their medications sorted out in those little Sunday-to-Saturday pill organizers. I'm the one holding it all together for them, just like I do for my clients at work. If anything, I worry about what would happen to them if I just... stopped. If I just couldn't push through this heaviness anymore and stayed in bed one morning. Who would make sure Mr. Abernathy got his shower? Who would make sure my mother-in-law didn't trip over the rug in the hallway? 

They rely on me so much. I think that's part of why I feel so incredibly drained all the time, because there's just no room for me to drop the ball. I can't be a burden, because there's no one else to take the weight if I let it go. So I just keep dragging myself through the mud, day after day, because they need me. It's just... it's just so much to carry, Doctor. It really is.
Do you feel like your lack of interest in activities is interfering with your daily life?

Interfering? Well, yes, I suppose it really is, when you put it that way. I mean, take my job, for instance. As a home health aide, you wouldn't believe the amount of paperwork we have to do. Every single time I visit a client, I have to fill out these incredibly detailed care logs—what they ate, their blood pressure, if they had a bowel movement, how their skin looks, all of it. I used to just knock it out right there at the kitchen table while they were eating lunch or watching their daytime stories. It was just part of the routine. 

But lately? I just... I don't have the drive to even pick up the pen. I just sit there staring at the forms, feeling completely blank. So I've started falling behind on my client documentation, which is so unlike me. I end up bringing the files home, and they just sit in a stack on my dining room table, right next to my mother-in-law's pill organizers, and I just look at them and feel this heavy dread. My supervisor actually had to call me about it last week because I was three days late submitting Mrs. Higgins' charts, which was honestly so embarrassing because I've always prided myself on being on top of things. 

And it’s not just the paperwork, either. It’s the people part of the job, too. I used to be the one the agency would always ask to train the new girls. I actually used to really enjoy it, you know? Showing them the ropes, explaining the best way to gently roll a bedbound patient, or how to redirect the clients with dementia so they don't get agitated. I used to volunteer to mentor the newer aides all the time. It gave me a sense of pride, I guess. But I just don't do that anymore. I actually told my manager last month that I couldn't take on any trainees for the foreseeable future. I just don't have the enthusiasm or the patience to explain things to a twenty-year-old who doesn't know how to properly lock a wheelchair.

Every last drop of energy. By the time I finish just the essential, non-negotiable tasks of the day, there is absolutely nothing left in the tank for anything extra. Headaches? Or muscle pain? Well... no, not really. I mean, my feet definitely ache at the end of the day, but I'm in my sensible shoes walking on hard tile and linoleum floors for eight to ten hours, so that's just to be expected. And, you know, when you're a home health aide helping someone transfer from their bed to their wheelchair, you are doing a fair bit of lifting. If I don't use the gait belt exactly right—which they always drill into us at our annual agency training, you know, "bend at the knees, keep your back straight"—my lower back might give a little twinge. But that's just poor body mechanics on my part, not an actual muscle ache from... well, from this mood I've been in. 

And headaches... no, I don't really get those either. My husband is the one who gets terrible tension headaches. He’ll come home from the auto parts store just rubbing his temples, squinting at the overhead lights in the kitchen, and I always have to make sure we have the big bottle of ibuprofen stocked in the downstairs bathroom for him. But for me? No, my head doesn't hurt. 

It's really just... it's more of an overall heaviness. Like my whole body is made of lead, or like I'm trying to walk through wet cement all day. It's not a sharp pain or a throbbing ache, it's just that my body feels so incredibly drained. I suppose I'm actually quite lucky I don't get headaches on top of everything else, because if my head was pounding while I was trying to concentrate on those detailed care logs I mentioned, or while listening to my mother-in-law's walker clank down the hallway at two in the morning... well, I just don't know how I would manage that. I mean, I was working my regular shifts, driving all over the county taking care of my clients, and then coming home to basically do the exact same job for her—managing her pill organizers, getting her meals ready, making sure she was comfortable. It was a lot. But even after we finally got into a steady routine and the physical exhaustion sort of settled down, that joy just never came back. 

So it's been a little over two solid years of this. Two whole years of setting up my scrapbook paper or cooking a nice meal and just feeling absolutely nothing. It's like the weekend we moved her boxes into that spare room, my ability to actually enjoy my own life just got packed away too. It's been a long two years of just going through the motions like that.

inference.note: Added F32.1 as the patient's symptoms of anhedonia and loss of interest in activities suggest a depressive episode, but the duration and other specifics are still being clarified

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels or the way you move throughout the day?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By the time I finish seeing my home-health clients and come back to help at home, my body feels heavy and even charting notes or folding laundry can feel like too much to push through.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in energy levels, which directly corresponds to the symptom of fatigue.

patient.answer:
Energy levels? Oh, goodness... yes. Yes, absolutely. It’s actually been a real struggle lately. I mean, my days have always been long, but it feels so different now. You know I do home health care, so I'm usually out the door by 6:30 or 7:00 in the morning, driving all over the county. And it's physical work, too—helping people out of bed, assisting with showers, transferring them from the bed to their recliners. I have one client, Mr. Abernathy, who is a fairly large man, and helping him takes a lot out of me. But I used to handle it all just fine. I used to have the stamina for it.

Now, though... by the time I finish seeing my home-health clients for the day and I pull into my own driveway, I usually just sit in the car for a few minutes. I just sit there with the engine off because I know I have to go inside and start helping out at home with my mother-in-law. And when I finally make myself get out of the car and walk through that front door, my body just feels so incredibly heavy. That's the only way I can describe it. Like my arms and legs are filled with wet sand or lead. 

It gets to the point where even the smallest, most basic tasks feel like climbing a mountain. I have to do my charting every evening, you know, writing up my notes for the agency on my tablet so they have a record of the clients' vitals and everything. I used to just sit at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and knock it out in fifteen minutes. Now, even just opening the app and charting those notes can feel like entirely too much to push through. I'll just stare at the screen, resting my head in my hand, feeling like I can't even type. 

And the laundry! Oh, the laundry. Between my husband's work clothes and my mother-in-law's things, there is always a basket waiting. I'll look at a pile of clean towels on the sofa—just simple folding, right? Nothing strenuous at all. But I just look at it and feel like I physically cannot lift my arms to fold a single washcloth. The energy just isn't there anymore. I just feel so weighed down and completely drained, like I'm dragging myself through mud just to get through the evening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving or worsening over time
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your symptoms over the past few months, either getting better or worse?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the general course or progression of my symptoms (whether they are getting better or worse over the past few months), which is not covered by any specific symptom profile in my list.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about the last few months specifically. You know, since maybe around the holidays? It's... it's hard to say, really, because all the days just seem to bleed together lately. But to answer your question, no, I wouldn't say things have gotten worse, but they certainly haven't gotten any better either. It's just this constant, flat line. Every single day feels exactly the same. I wake up, I go see my clients, I come home to my mother-in-law, I stare at the laundry... it's honestly a bit like that movie Groundhog Day, if you've ever seen it. Just waking up and doing the exact same heavy, exhausting routine without any spark of joy, day in and day out. 

I keep hoping, you know, that maybe with the seasons changing, or maybe if I just got one solid, uninterrupted night of sleep things might lift a little. My mother-in-law, she gets up a lot in the night to use the restroom, and she has one of those aluminum walkers with the tennis balls on the back legs? And our hallway is hardwood, so I can hear that *scuff, scuff, scuff* sound at 2 AM, and once I'm awake, I'm just awake, staring at the ceiling, thinking about everything I have to do the next day. But even on the rare nights where she actually sleeps straight through till dawn, I still wake up feeling just as drained and just as numb as I always do. 

So, no, I haven't noticed any real shift up or down in how I'm feeling. It's just a steady plateau of... well, of nothingness, really. Just this heavy nothingness that doesn't budge an inch. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, maybe just one day where I feel a little lighter or have a little more pep in my step, but it just hasn't happened. It's been remarkably, frustratingly consistent.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that aren't there when you're alone?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms (hallucinations), which are not covered by any item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Voices? Or seeing things? Oh, no, no. Goodness, no. Nothing like that. I mean, honestly, Doctor, I’m rarely ever truly alone to even know what that would be like! Between driving to my clients' houses all day and then coming home to my husband and my mother-in-law, there is almost always someone talking to me or needing something from me. 

But no, when I am actually by myself—like in the car on the drive home, which is about the only twenty minutes of peace I get all day—it’s just quiet. Well, I say quiet, but usually I'm just sitting there listening to the hum of the engine or the radio playing softly in the background, just going over the grocery list in my head or trying to figure out when I'm going to find time to pick up my mother-in-law's blood pressure prescriptions. But as for hearing people talking who aren't there, or seeing things? No. 

I actually have a couple of clients in my home health work—older folks, mostly the ones further along with dementia—who do experience that sort of thing. I had this one sweet lady last year, Mrs. Higgins, who used to talk to her late husband in the corner of the living room the entire time I was fixing her lunch. She would point right at the armchair and ask him if he wanted a sandwich. So I've seen what that looks like firsthand, and I know exactly what you're asking about, but I've never experienced anything like that myself. My mind is just... well, it's just heavy with my own thoughts, but they're definitely just my own thoughts. Just the regular, exhausting worries of the day, nothing out of the ordinary like that.

inference.note: F43.0 was ruled out due to lack of traumatic or stressful events and no clear evidence of adjustment disorder

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're a burden to your loved ones?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or being a burden, which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
A burden? Oh, goodness... no. No, I wouldn't say I feel like a burden. Honestly, it's quite the opposite. I'm the one carrying everyone else, you know? I mean, my husband works hard, he really does, he's at the auto parts store all day, but when he gets home, he's just done. He sits in his recliner, turns on the evening news, and that's it for him. He doesn't really notice what needs doing around the house. And then there's his mother, my mother-in-law, who lives with us. I love her, I really do, but she needs so much help. She can't stand at the stove to cook anymore, she needs help getting her compression socks on in the mornings, and like I mentioned, she's up and down all night with that walker. 

So, no, I don't feel like a burden to them because I'm the one making sure they have clean clothes, hot meals, and their medications sorted out in those little Sunday-to-Saturday pill organizers. I'm the one holding it all together for them, just like I do for my clients at work. If anything, I worry about what would happen to them if I just... stopped. If I just couldn't push through this heaviness anymore and stayed in bed one morning. Who would make sure Mr. Abernathy got his shower? Who would make sure my mother-in-law didn't trip over the rug in the hallway? 

They rely on me so much. I think that's part of why I feel so incredibly drained all the time, because there's just no room for me to drop the ball. I can't be a burden, because there's no one else to take the weight if I let it go. So I just keep dragging myself through the mud, day after day, because they need me. It's just... it's just so much to carry, Doctor. It really is.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like your lack of interest in activities is interfering with your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've started falling behind on my client documentation and I don't volunteer to mentor newer aides the way I used to, because just keeping up with the basics at work and at home takes everything I have.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the lack of interest is interfering with my daily life, which directly addresses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Interfering? Well, yes, I suppose it really is, when you put it that way. I mean, take my job, for instance. As a home health aide, you wouldn't believe the amount of paperwork we have to do. Every single time I visit a client, I have to fill out these incredibly detailed care logs—what they ate, their blood pressure, if they had a bowel movement, how their skin looks, all of it. I used to just knock it out right there at the kitchen table while they were eating lunch or watching their daytime stories. It was just part of the routine. 

But lately? I just... I don't have the drive to even pick up the pen. I just sit there staring at the forms, feeling completely blank. So I've started falling behind on my client documentation, which is so unlike me. I end up bringing the files home, and they just sit in a stack on my dining room table, right next to my mother-in-law's pill organizers, and I just look at them and feel this heavy dread. My supervisor actually had to call me about it last week because I was three days late submitting Mrs. Higgins' charts, which was honestly so embarrassing because I've always prided myself on being on top of things. 

And it’s not just the paperwork, either. It’s the people part of the job, too. I used to be the one the agency would always ask to train the new girls. I actually used to really enjoy it, you know? Showing them the ropes, explaining the best way to gently roll a bedbound patient, or how to redirect the clients with dementia so they don't get agitated. I used to volunteer to mentor the newer aides all the time. It gave me a sense of pride, I guess. But I just don't do that anymore. I actually told my manager last month that I couldn't take on any trainees for the foreseeable future. I just don't have the enthusiasm or the patience to explain things to a twenty-year-old who doesn't know how to properly lock a wheelchair. 

It's just that keeping up with the bare minimum—the absolute basics of making sure my clients are safe and clean, and then coming home and making sure my husband and mother-in-law have dinner and clean clothes—it takes everything I have. Every last drop of energy. By the time I finish just the essential, non-negotiable tasks of the day, there is absolutely nothing left in the tank for anything extra. Not for paperwork, not for teaching, not for anything. So, yes, I'd definitely say it's interfering, because I'm really just barely scraping by on the absolute minimum right now.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for F32.0 (Mild depressive episode) or F32.1 (Moderate depressive episode) based on the presence of somatic symptoms
doctor.question: Do you experience any physical symptoms like headaches or muscle pain in addition to your low mood?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms such as headaches or muscle pain, which are not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles (which include depressed mood, weight/appetite change, sleep disturbance, and fatigue).

patient.answer:
Headaches? Or muscle pain? Well... no, not really. I mean, my feet definitely ache at the end of the day, but I'm in my sensible shoes walking on hard tile and linoleum floors for eight to ten hours, so that's just to be expected. And, you know, when you're a home health aide helping someone transfer from their bed to their wheelchair, you are doing a fair bit of lifting. If I don't use the gait belt exactly right—which they always drill into us at our annual agency training, you know, "bend at the knees, keep your back straight"—my lower back might give a little twinge. But that's just poor body mechanics on my part, not an actual muscle ache from... well, from this mood I've been in. 

And headaches... no, I don't really get those either. My husband is the one who gets terrible tension headaches. He’ll come home from the auto parts store just rubbing his temples, squinting at the overhead lights in the kitchen, and I always have to make sure we have the big bottle of ibuprofen stocked in the downstairs bathroom for him. But for me? No, my head doesn't hurt. 

It's really just... it's more of an overall heaviness. Like my whole body is made of lead, or like I'm trying to walk through wet cement all day. It's not a sharp pain or a throbbing ache, it's just that my body feels so incredibly drained. I suppose I'm actually quite lucky I don't get headaches on top of everything else, because if my head was pounding while I was trying to concentrate on those detailed care logs I mentioned, or while listening to my mother-in-law's walker clank down the hallway at two in the morning... well, I just don't know how I would manage that. It would be the straw that broke the camel's back. So, no, no physical pain like that. Just that utter, heavy exhaustion.
